districts.name: Northwest
districts.intro: District 1 is San Francisco's northwest quarter — the long grid of the Richmond running from Arguello out to Ocean Beach, bounded by the Presidio above and Golden Gate Park below. It is a district of wide, flat avenues and solid pre-war stock: Edwardian flats and marina-style homes on 25-foot lots, giving way to the large detached houses and ocean frontage of Sea Cliff and Lake Street.

districts.name: Central West
districts.intro: District 2 is the Sunset and Parkside — the largest contiguous residential district in San Francisco and, by volume, its busiest single-family market. The stock is remarkably consistent: rows of 1930s and 1940s tunnel-entrance houses on a regular grid, most with garages below and level entries, running from Golden Gate Park south to Sloat and west to the ocean.

districts.name: Southwest
districts.intro: District 3 is the city's southwest corner — Lakeside, Ingleside, Oceanview and the blocks around Lake Merced and San Francisco State. It is among the most attainable single-family markets in San Francisco, with a mix of 1920s bungalows, post-war tract housing and larger lots than the districts to the north.

districts.name: Twin Peaks West
districts.intro: District 4 is the arc of planned residence parks on the western slope of Twin Peaks — St Francis Wood, Forest Hill, Balboa Terrace, Westwood Park and their neighbours. Laid out in the 1910s and 1920s with curving streets, mature street trees and design covenants, these are the closest thing San Francisco has to garden suburbs, and the stock is correspondingly large.

districts.name: Central
districts.intro: District 5 is the geographic and, for many buyers, the emotional center of San Francisco — the belt of hillside neighborhoods running from Haight Ashbury and Cole Valley east through the Castro and Mission Dolores, then south into Noe Valley and Glen Park. It is a district of Victorians and Edwardians on steep streets, of view lots on Corona Heights and Clarendon Heights, and of the flatter, family-scaled blocks below Noe Valley's 24th Street corridor.

districts.name: Central North
districts.intro: District 6 runs across the middle of the city's northern half — Hayes Valley, Alamo Square, the North Panhandle and the Western Addition. It is one of the densest districts in San Francisco and overwhelmingly a flats-and-condominium market; detached single-family houses are the exception here rather than the rule, which is why the figures below rest on a small number of sales.

districts.name: North
districts.intro: District 7 is the city's most expensive district and has been for a long time — Pacific Heights, Presidio Heights, Cow Hollow and the Marina, running along the northern waterfront from the Presidio to Van Ness. The stock ranges from Marina-style flats on the flat blocks near the bay to the very large detached houses on the Pacific Heights crest, where the Golden Gate views are.

districts.name: Northeast
districts.intro: District 8 covers the city's dense northeast corner — Russian Hill, Nob Hill, Telegraph Hill, North Beach and the Financial District. It is the most vertical district in San Francisco and almost entirely a condominium and co-operative market; the handful of detached single-family sales each quarter are unusual properties, so the figures below describe a very small slice of what actually trades here.

districts.name: Central East
districts.intro: District 9 is the city's eastern flank — the Mission, Potrero Hill, Bernal Heights, Dogpatch, SoMa and Mission Bay. It is the district that has changed most in the past two decades, pairing intact Victorian and Edwardian blocks in the Mission and on Bernal with wholly new construction on the former railyards and waterfront to the east.

districts.name: Southeast
districts.intro: District 10 is the southeast quarter — Bayview, Hunters Point, the Excelsior, Portola and Visitacion Valley. It is the most attainable single-family district in San Francisco and, by sale count, one of the busiest: the stock is overwhelmingly detached houses on standard lots, much of it built between the 1920s and the 1950s, on some of the sunniest ground in the city.
